strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and interesting: constructing an algebraically reversible solver for diffusion SDEs by exploiting the time-symmetry of the Stratonovich integral, the Dambis–Dubins–Schwarz time-change to a Brownian bridge, and the Brownian interval (Kidger et al., 2021) so that the Wiener realization never needs to be stored in memory. This addresses a real gap, as prior exact-inversion work for SDEs (Wu & De la Torre, 2022) requires storing the full noise realization.

The derivation in Proposition 4.1 and Appendix B is a clean application of exponential integrators and time-changed Brownian motion to the reverse-time diffusion SDE, and the proof is worked through in reasonable detail.

The paper situates itself well relative to related work, including a clear explanation (Appendix A) of why Wu & De la Torre (2022) is memory-inefficient, and an honest limitations section acknowledging the preliminary nature of the work.
The motivating discussion of truncation error alignment and two-sided numerical stability is a useful framing that existing ODE-inversion methods (EDICT, BI, BELM) do not fully address.
weaknesses: The central 'exact inversion' claim rests on the assumption that the data prediction model is trained to zero loss (x_hat_0|t = x_0|t). Real score networks have substantial approximation error, and the paper provides no analysis or experiments showing how model error degrades reversibility. Without this, the headline claim is only exact for an idealized model, and the practical significance is unclear.

The empirical evaluation is a single qualitative figure on face interpolation with one LDM model (CelebA-HQ) and 20 steps. There are no quantitative metrics (inversion reconstruction error, FID, LPIPS, memory footprint), no ablations (e.g., sensitivity to the coupling parameter ζ, number of steps, order of the Stratonovich–Taylor expansion), and no error bars or multiple examples. Claims like 'less visible distortions' are not measurable from one panel.

The baseline comparison is deliberately weakened: the authors state DDIM inversion was run at a low step count 'on purpose to stress test the solvers,' which is a strawman setting since DDIM inversion is known to be accurate with more steps. There is also no memory/runtime comparison against Wu & De la Torre (2022), which is the most relevant prior SDE-inversion method and the one the memory claim is made against.

The motivation section prominently raises two-sided numerical stability and continuous-adjoint applications, but the paper contains no stability analysis (the 'region of convergence' behavior of the coupled scheme is never characterized beyond the citation of McCallum & Foster, 2024) and no adjoint/guidance experiments, leaving the motivating applications untested.

Practical usability of the augmented state x_hat is not discussed: for editing/interpolation tasks the user must also interpolate the auxiliary state x_hat, which is an unnatural latent artifact of the reversible construction; this limitation is not analyzed.

Writing and presentation issues: several typos ('methodvariation-of-parameters', 'The we express', 'Harier' for Hairer, 'Telsa'), Equation (4.1)'s sign conventions and the two-sided-filtration footnote are subtle and could confuse readers, and the quadratic-variation computation in Eq. (B.18) is presented with a sign slip (the intermediate expression is written negative before being named positive ςt), which undermines confidence in the proof as written.
No code or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and experimental details (exact solver settings, schedules, ζ values beyond 0.999) are thin, making independent verification difficult.

strengths: Genuinely novel direction: the paper appears to be the first to propose exact (algebraic) inversion for diffusion SDEs that avoids storing the full Wiener process realization, building cleverly on the Brownian interval (Kidger et al., 2021) and the reversibility-by-construction idea of McCallum & Foster (2024).

The core mathematical development is substantive: the conversion of the reverse-time SDE to a Stratonovich integral equation, the variation-of-parameters/exponential-integrator reduction (Proposition 4.1), and the Dubins-Schwarz time-change argument in Appendix B are worked out in reasonable detail and mostly check out for the additive-noise VP setting.

The motivation section (truncation error alignment and bidirectional stability) is clearly articulated and connects to concrete downstream applications (SDE-based editing, adjoint-gradient methods) that the SDE formulation is known to favor (Nie et al., 2024).
The limitations section is honest, explicitly framing the work as a proof of concept.
weaknesses: Severely insufficient empirical evidence. The entire experimental validation is a single qualitative figure (one pair of faces, one model, one dataset, 20 steps) with no quantitative metrics whatsoever: no inversion reconstruction error, no LPIPS/FID, no memory or runtime comparison against storing the noise (e.g., Wu & De la Torre, 2022), and no ablation over the coupling parameter ζ despite it being the central stability knob.

The headline claim of 'exact inversion' is only demonstrated visually. The algebraic reversibility of Eqs. (4.3)-(4.4) is asserted but never verified numerically (e.g., round-trip error down to float precision), and the assumed zero-loss data prediction model (x̂_0|t = x_0|t) never holds in practice; the paper does not analyze how score-approximation error interacts with the reversibility of the coupled scheme.

Several technical points are under-justified: (i) the backward pass Eq. (4.4) is stated without derivation or proof of correctness, including the peculiar ζ^{-1}-scaling of the noise term; (ii) the initialization of the augmented state x̂ (e.g., x̂_N at t=T) is not specified; (iii) the subtlety of using a two-sided filtration / non-adapted Stratonovich integral in the sampling procedure deserves more care than a footnote.

The stability analysis motivating the work ('alignment in truncation errors... reasonable numerical stability in both directions') is promised but never delivered, even for the linear test equation; the abstract and introduction oversell capabilities (editing, adjoint gradients) that are never tested.

Presentation is sloppy for a main-track submission: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('methodvariation-of-parameters', 'The we express', 'Harier' for Hairer, 'Telsa'), an unexplained Eq. (B.15) that appears after the derivation has already concluded, inconsistent notation (x_0|t vs x_0|τ in Eq. B.6), and a main text of roughly four pages that reads like a workshop/work-in-progress paper.
No code or reproducibility artifacts are provided; the experimental details (Appendix C) amount to three sentences, making independent verification difficult.

Significance is currently limited: without quantitative evidence that the SDE solver's claimed advantages over ODE inversion (e.g., vs. EDICT, BELM, Zhang et al. 2024) materialize in practice, the practical usefulness over existing exact ODE inversion methods remains speculative.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and well-motivated: extending exact diffusion inversion from the ODE setting (EDICT, BIA, BELM) to the SDE setting, which Nie et al. (2024) argue is preferable for latent editing, and doing so without storing the full Wiener process realization (in contrast to Wu & De la Torre, 2022).

The mathematical development is reasonably careful: the derivation of the exact solution (Proposition 4.1) via variation-of-parameters, exponential integrators, the Fisk-Stratonovich reformulation (justified since the noise is additive), and the Dubins-Schwarz time-change yielding the Brownian bridge term is clean and the full proof in Appendix B is verifiable.

The construction of the reversible solver is sensibly grounded in prior theory (Brownian interval from Kidger et al. 2021; coupling-parameter trick from McCallum & Foster 2024), and the related-work discussion (Appendix A) correctly situates the contribution relative to ODE inversion and prior SDE inversion.
The paper is honest in its limitations section, acknowledging that the experiments are proof-of-concept only.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is far too thin to support the central claims. The entire experimental section is a single qualitative figure (one interpolation example on faces). There are no quantitative inversion-error measurements (e.g., reconstruction MSE or LPIPS between the re-decoded original image and the round-trip reconstruction), no ablation over the coupling parameter ζ or step count, and only one image is shown. 'Exact inversion' and 'performs better than ODE-based inversion' are claims that require quantitative backing, especially since the visual differences in Figure 1c vs 1b are subtle.

The headline practical benefit — not storing the full Wiener realization — is never measured. There is no memory or runtime comparison against Wu & De la Torre (2022), which is the closest prior method and the natural baseline. Without this, the paper's distinguishing contribution over existing SDE inversion is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The main theoretical result assumes the data prediction model is trained to zero loss (x̂_{0|t} = x_{0|t}), which is unrealistic in practice. The paper does not analyze how model approximation error interacts with the algebraic reversibility or the claimed alignment of truncation errors, even though this is exactly the regime where reversibility matters (real pretrained models).

The coupling parameter ζ is central to the solver's stability properties (per McCallum & Foster 2024), yet no stability analysis is given for the SDE setting, and ζ = 0.999 is used with no justification. The motivation section promises 'reasonable numerical stability in both directions' but this is never analyzed or empirically characterized.

The solver Ψ_h (the single-step approximation of the exponential integral via truncated Stratonovich-Taylor expansion) is not specified anywhere — only 'first-order' is mentioned. Combined with the unspecified initialization of the augmented state x̂_0 and the absence of any code release, reproducibility is poor.

There are presentation defects that undermine confidence: typos such as 'methodvariation-of-parameters' and 'The we express' in the proof sketch, 'Telsa V100', and inconsistent claims about what is 'exact' (the Brownian bridge and linear terms are exact, but the overall scheme is of course approximate — the paper is sometimes careless in wording).

The downstream usefulness of exact SDE inversion (guided generation via continuous adjoint equations, image editing) — the stated motivation — is not demonstrated at all, so the significance beyond the interpolation proof-of-concept remains speculative.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and original: combining Lawson methods (exponential integrators) with the McCallum-Foster reversible solver framework yields the first algebraically reversible solver family for diffusion models that (i) attains arbitrarily high order for the probability-flow ODE, (ii) applies to both ODE and reverse-time SDE formulations, and (iii) achieves exact SDE inversion without storing the entire Brownian trajectory, using splittable PRNG techniques from the neural SDE literature.

The theoretical treatment is careful and complete: time-reparameterization propositions for both data- and noise-prediction parameterizations (Propositions 3.1, 3.2), full derivation of the scheme (Proposition 3.3, Appendix C), convergence order proofs (Theorems 4.1, 4.2), and a stability analysis. The provenance of results (e.g., inheriting order from McCallum-Foster via change of variables) is transparent.

Appendix E provides a genuinely valuable unifying result (Theorem E.1): the Lawson construction subsumes DDIM, DPM-Solver-1/2/12, DPM-Solver++ variants, SDE-DPM-Solvers, SEEDS-1, and gDDIM, so Rex yields reversible versions of these widely used samplers. This gives the paper significance beyond a single new solver.

Appendix A contains a thorough and useful comparative analysis of prior reversible/inversion methods (EDICT, BDIA, BELM), including new observations that BDIA and O-BELM reduce to the leapfrog/midpoint method and are nowhere linearly stable.

The paper is unusually honest about limitations: Appendix J documents failure cases (data-prediction latent variance blowing up to ~10^7, ShARK overflow errors, ODE-based interpolation artifacts), and these are surfaced rather than hidden.
Reproducibility is addressed well: full derivations, implementation details, noise-schedule inverse functions, hardware, and lists of all repositories and model checkpoints used.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is limited in scope and the results are mixed. On CelebA-HQ FID (Table 1), the non-reversible DDIM baseline (20.96 at 50 steps) is essentially on par with the best Rex variant (19.77), and O-BELM beats Rex at 10 and 20 steps. On Stable Diffusion (Table 2), differences in CLIP score and ImageReward between methods are small. The central practical benefit of Rex over existing reversible samplers is therefore not convincingly demonstrated.

The headline claim of 'arbitrarily high order of convergence' is not borne out in practice: Table 4 shows the high-order Rex (RK4) variants performing comparably to or worse than lower-order ones at few steps, with the midpoint variant failing entirely at 10 steps, and the authors resort to replacing the last two steps with Euler/Euler-Maruyama for stability. This suggests a gap between the theory and the practical regime (very few steps) where diffusion samplers matter most.

Several practical fragilities are acknowledged but not systematically resolved: the time interval must be shrunk to [epsilon, 1] for stability, the coupling parameter zeta requires tuning, the data-prediction formulation of Rex (Euler) produces latent variances many orders of magnitude too large, and ODE-based interpolation 'fails quite noticeably'. No principled guidance or sensitivity analysis for zeta is provided.

The theoretical contributions, while correct, are largely transplantations: the convergence-order theorems follow almost immediately from McCallum-Foster's theorem combined with norm-bounded changes of variables, and the time reparameterizations are variants of known stochastic exponential time-differencing. The novelty is in the combination and the SDE reversibility, not in deep new analysis.
No release of the authors' own implementation is stated; only third-party repositories are cited, which weakens reproducibility despite the detailed appendices.

Evaluation is confined to two models (a DDPM on CelebA-HQ 256x256 and SD v1.5) with 1000-10240 samples; no higher-resolution, newer, or flow-matching models, and no downstream inversion-dependent applications (e.g., editing, image-to-image) are quantitatively evaluated, even though exact inversion is the motivating use case.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly-articulated gap: to the authors' knowledge (and mine) there is no algebraically reversible solver for diffusion SDEs that does not store the entire Brownian path, and the proposed Rex construction (Lawson methods applied to reparameterized ODEs/SDEs wrapped in the McCallum–Foster coupling) is a principled way to fill it.

The technical treatment is rigorous and unusually complete: the time reparameterization of the reverse-time SDE (Proposition 3.2) is proved carefully via the Dambis–Dubins–Schwarz theorem, the use of space-time Lévy areas from Foster et al. (2024) yields a strong-order-1.5 stochastic scheme (contrasting with SEEDS' weak order 1), and convergence-order results (Theorems 4.1, 4.2) are proved for both parameterizations.

Appendix E provides a valuable unifying perspective, showing that Rex's underlying scheme subsumes DDIM, DPM-Solver variants, SEEDS-1 and gDDIM as reversible versions, and Appendix A cleanly proves that EDICT and BDIA/O-BELM are zeroth/first-order and nowhere linearly stable — this is useful analysis for the community beyond the proposed method.

Reproducibility is taken seriously: detailed derivations, implementation details, noise-schedule inverses in closed form, and full experimental setup are provided, and limitations (e.g., instability of the data-prediction formulation, the ShARK failure case in Figure 9) are documented honestly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The empirical case for the method is unconvincing. On the flagship FID comparison (Table 1), Rex (RK4) is clearly worse than the O-BELM baseline at 10 and 20 steps (31.00 vs 27.16; 23.49 vs 20.15) and essentially tied at 50 steps, so the advertised arbitrarily-high order does not translate into a practical sampling advantage. Table 2 shows similarly marginal differences on CLIP/Image Reward.

The headline claim — exact SDE inversion without storing the Brownian path — is supported only qualitatively (Figures 3, 5, and the interpolation study). There is no quantitative metric of inversion fidelity/reconstruction error, no downstream application (editing, guidance, morphs) where the SDE bijection is actually exploited, despite the introduction motivating inversion through such applications.

Much of the theoretical machinery is inherited: the order-preservation of the reversible wrapper is a direct adaptation of McCallum & Foster (2024, Theorem 2.1), and the exponential-integrator/Lawson reparameterizations are well established in the diffusion literature (DPM-Solver, SEEDS). The novelty is primarily in the combination and the SDE extension rather than in new tools.

Practical restrictions are significant and under-discussed in the main text: adaptive step sizes are prohibited (footnote 7), an auxiliary state must be stored, the data-prediction formulation is numerically unstable in practice (Appendix J), and the ShARK SDE variant can overflow and lose reversibility entirely (Figure 9).

The experimental scope is narrow: one unconditional DDPM on CelebA-HQ 256 and Stable Diffusion v1.5 with 1000 COCO captions. No higher-resolution or more modern models, no variance/repeats across seeds for the metric tables, and no ablation on the coupling parameter ζ beyond isolated remarks.

The main text is dense and notation-heavy (three time variables ζ, ϱ, χ plus weighting terms w_n and an auxiliary state x̃), which makes the core solver (Proposition 3.3) hard to parse; much of the intuition is relegated to a computation-graph figure and appendices.

strengths: The paper makes a genuine and clearly stated contribution: a family of algebraically reversible solvers (Rex) for diffusion models that works for both the probability-flow ODE and the reverse-time SDE, and — to the authors' credit — appears to be the first scheme enabling exact SDE inversion without storing the full Brownian trajectory.

The theoretical treatment is unusually thorough for this area: convergence-order results (Theorems 4.1/4.2) are proved for both ODE and SRK cases, stability is analyzed (with honest acknowledgement that reversible solvers are generally unstable and that Rex inherits a non-trivial stability region from McCallum-Foster), and the unifying Propositions/Theorem E.1 showing that Rex subsumes DDIM, DPM-Solver variants, gDDIM, and SEEDS-1 as reversible counterparts is a valuable unifying perspective that connects previously disparate lines of work.

The mathematical development is careful and largely self-contained: the time-reparameterization derivations via the Dambis-Dubins-Schwarz theorem, the use of Lawson methods and space-time Lévy areas (ShARK), and the closed-form inverses for common noise schedules (Appendix H) are all worked out in detail, which aids reproducibility.

Empirical evaluation covers unconditional generation (CelebA-HQ with FID), conditional text-to-image (Stable Diffusion with CLIP score and Image Reward), and interpolation, with honest reporting of failure cases (e.g., Figure 9 'FAILURE CASE!' and the instability analysis in Appendix J), which is commendable transparency.

The related-work section (Appendix A) provides a genuinely useful comparison table (Table 3) of reversible solvers in terms of extra states, truncation error, stability, and convergence proofs, and cleanly positions Rex against EDICT, BDIA, and BELM.
weaknesses: The headline practical benefit over existing methods is marginal. In Table 1, O-BELM outperforms Rex (RK4) at 10 and 20 steps, and the best Rex variant at 50 steps (FID 19.77) is barely better than the non-reversible DDIM baseline (20.96). In Table 2, DDIM achieves the best CLIP scores at all step counts, and Image Reward gains over O-BELM/BDIA are small. This weakens the case that Rex is preferable as a general-purpose sampler, leaving exact reversibility as the main selling point.

The paper's central motivation — that exact inversion enables downstream applications — is under-demonstrated. Beyond a qualitative interpolation experiment (Section 5.2, no quantitative comparison), no editing, reconstruction-fidelity, or morphing benchmarks are provided, so the practical value of the reversibility property remains largely untested. The Appendix J analysis revealing latent-variance blow-ups (data prediction) and artefacts/non-Gaussianity (noise prediction) further limits confidence in the inversion machinery for real applications.

The convergence-order results are relatively modest generalizations: Theorem 4.1 and 4.2 essentially follow from McCallum & Foster (2024, Theorem 2.1) plus a change-of-variables and a boundedness argument on σ_t/α_t; the proofs (Appendix D) are short and the assumptions (variance-preserving schedules, α_T > 0) restrict generality without discussion of extensions to e.g. VE or sub-VP schedules.

Fixed-step-size integration is inherent to the method (the paper notes this 'clearly prohibits the use of adaptive step-size solvers', footnote 7), and the coupling parameter ζ plus last-step Euler/Euler-Maruyama hacks (Appendix I.2) introduce hyperparameters whose sensitivity is not ablated.
No evidence of a released codebase is provided (only third-party repositories used), which limits reproducibility of the exact experimental setup despite the detailed derivations.

Writing is at times dense and notation-heavy (multiple reparameterizations γ, ϱ, χ, ξ with parallel data/noise-prediction versions), which may impede adoption even by readers well-versed in diffusion samplers.
